items.name: Ampelmännchen
clues: It tells you when to stop and when to go, but it never says a word.
Everyone who walks around eastern Germany, and lots of tourists who take it home as a souvenir.
A traffic psychologist suggested it in East Berlin in 1961, and his secretary drew it.
A little figure with a short body, a big nose and a hat. It comes in red and in green.
Its hat came from a photo of the East German leader Erich Honecker in a summer straw hat. In the 1990s people campaigned to save it.
Its German name means “little traffic-light man”.

items.name: London Underground map
clues: It helps millions of people get from A to B every day, but it isn't really true.
Commuters, tourists, and anyone who has ever been lost under a big city.
An engineering draughtsman drew it in his free time in 1931, after losing his job. It became the official map in 1933.
Only straight lines and 45-degree angles, and a different colour for every line.
It ignores real distances. The idea came from electrical circuit diagrams.
It shows every station on the world's oldest underground railway, in the British capital.

items.name: Juicy Salif
clues: It does one small job in the kitchen, but it looks as if it came from outer space.
Design fans who want something to talk about on their kitchen counter.
A French designer sketched it on a napkin while he was eating a plate of squid and squeezing lemon over it. It came out around 1990.
Shiny aluminium, a pointed body and three long, thin legs, a bit like a spider or a rocket.
Its designer said it was “not meant to squeeze lemons” but “to start conversations”.
A lemon squeezer by Philippe Starck for the Italian company Alessi.

items.name: Moka pot
clues: Every morning it makes a noise like a tiny steam train, and then everyone in the flat wakes up.
Millions of Italian families, and pretty much every student kitchen in Berlin.
It was born in a metal workshop in northern Italy in the 1930s.
An eight-sided aluminium body, a black handle and a little lid on top.
Its logo is a cartoon of a little man with a big moustache. When the boss of the company died in 2016, his ashes were put in one.
An Italian stovetop coffee maker by Bialetti: water in the bottom, coffee in the middle.

items.name: Rubik's Cube
clues: It's a toy, a puzzle and a sport. The fastest people finish it in a few seconds.
Children, maths fans, and people who leave it on their desk to look clever.
A Hungarian teacher of design and architecture made the first one in Budapest in 1974.
A small block with six sides: white, red, blue, orange, green and yellow.
It has about 43 quintillion possible positions, but only one of them is right.
A twisting colour puzzle named after its inventor, Ernő Rubik.

items.name: Lego brick
clues: It's very small and very simple, and it really hurts if you step on it with bare feet.
Children, and adults who buy the biggest sets “for their children”.
A carpenter started making wooden toys in a small Danish town in 1932.
A plastic block with round studs on top and tubes underneath.
Bricks made in 1958 still click together with bricks made today.
Its name comes from the Danish words “leg godt”, which mean “play well”.
